data.text/markdown:
Denavit-Hartenberg parameters

A robot arm is a chain of rigid links joined by joints. To know where its tool is, we attach a coordinate frame to every link and write the pose of each frame relative to the previous one. A general 3D pose needs six numbers, but the Denavit-Hartenberg (DH) convention places the frames so cleverly that four numbers per link are enough: ||(\theta_i||), ||(d_i||), ||(a_i||) and ||(\alpha_i||). This notebook uses the MRPT Python wheel (pip install mrpt3): each link transformation is an mrpt.poses.CPose3D, and chaining links is pose composition ||(\oplus||) (the + operator). It shows:
  1. The four elementary motions of one link, step by step.
  2. The rules to place the frames, and how to read the parameters off a drawing.
  3. The DH tables of classic manipulators, drawn frame by frame.
  4. An editable table to check your own exercises.
Next steps: forward kinematics and inverse kinematics.

1. One link: four elementary motions

In the standard DH convention, frame ||(i||) is reached from frame ||(i-1||) with four motions, each one along or about an axis of the frame obtained so far: ||[A_i = \mathrm{Rot}_z(\theta_i)\; \mathrm{Trans}_z(d_i)\; \mathrm{Trans}_x(a_i)\; \mathrm{Rot}_x(\alpha_i)||]
  1. Rotate ||(\theta_i||) about ||(z_{i-1}||): the joint angle.
  2. Move ||(d_i||) along ||(z_{i-1}||): the link offset.
  3. Move ||(a_i||) along the new ||(x||) axis, which is already ||(x_i||): the link length.
  4. Rotate ||(\alpha_i||) about ||(x_i||): the link twist, which turns the old ||(z||) axis into ||(z_i||).
The first two motions commute, and so do the last two, so in MRPT a link is the composition of just two poses, each one a translation plus a rotation: CPose3D(0, 0, d, θ, 0, 0) + CPose3D(a, 0, 0, 0, 0, α) (the arguments are x, y, z, yaw, pitch, roll; yaw turns about ||(z||) and roll about ||(x||)). Move the sliders, and use the last one to apply the motions one at a time.

Closed form (with ||(c_\theta = \cos\theta_i||), ||(s_\alpha = \sin\alpha_i||)...) ||[A_i = \begin{bmatrix} c_\theta & -s_\theta c_\alpha & s_\theta s_\alpha & a_i c_\theta \\ s_\theta & c_\theta c_\alpha & -c_\theta s_\alpha & a_i s_\theta \\ 0 & s_\alpha & c_\alpha & d_i \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}||]
From MRPT dh_pose(...).getHomogeneousMatrix() ||[A_i = \begin{bmatrix}+0.766 & -0.321 & +0.557 & +0.613 \\ +0.643 & +0.383 & -0.663 & +0.514 \\ +0.000 & +0.866 & +0.500 & +0.400 \\ +0.000 & +0.000 & +0.000 & +1.000\end{bmatrix}||]Largest difference with the closed form: 2.2e-16. The last motion, alone, gives the same frame: 0.0e+00.

2. Placing the frames

Four numbers are enough only because each frame is placed following some rules. For a chain with joints ||(1, \dots, n||), frame ||(0||) is the base and frame ||(i||) is attached to link ||(i||), the one moved by joint ||(i||):
  • ||(z_{i-1}||) lies along the axis of joint ||(i||): the rotation axis of a revolute joint, or the sliding direction of a prismatic joint.
  • ||(x_i||) lies along the common normal of ||(z_{i-1}||) and ||(z_i||): the line perpendicular to both, pointing from ||(z_{i-1}||) towards ||(z_i||). The origin ||(o_i||) is where it meets ||(z_i||).
  • ||(y_i||) completes a right-handed frame.
With the frames in place, the parameters can be read off a drawing (in the figure above, the dashed lines are the joint axes):
Parameter Meaning Measured
||(a_i||), link length distance between ||(z_{i-1}||) and ||(z_i||) (orange) along ||(x_i||)
||(\alpha_i||), link twist angle from ||(z_{i-1}||) to ||(z_i||) about ||(x_i||)
||(d_i||), link offset distance from ||(o_{i-1}||) to the common normal (purple) along ||(z_{i-1}||)
||(\theta_i||), joint angle angle from ||(x_{i-1}||) to ||(x_i||) about ||(z_{i-1}||)
||(a_i||) and ||(\alpha_i||) describe the shape of the link and never change. Of ||(d_i||) and ||(\theta_i||), one is the joint variable ||(q_i||) (||(\theta_i||) for a revolute joint, ||(d_i||) for a prismatic one) and the other is constant. The rules leave some free choices:
  • If ||(z_{i-1}||) and ||(z_i||) are parallel, there are infinitely many common normals: pick the one that makes ||(d_i = 0||).
  • If they intersect, ||(a_i = 0||) and ||(x_i||) is perpendicular to the plane of both axes (either direction).
  • The base frame only needs ||(z_0||) along the first joint axis, and the last frame (the tool) is chosen freely.

3. DH tables of classic manipulators

Below are the DH tables of six robots, with lengths in meters and angles in degrees. ||(q_i||) marks the joint variables, shown at a sample configuration. Move the slider to build the robot frame by frame: the gray line is the chain of ||(d_i||) and ||(a_i||) segments, and the circles (revolute) and diamonds (prismatic) mark the joints, on the ||(z||) axis of the previous frame.

4. Your own DH table

Write one link per line: the joint type (R or P), then ||(\theta||) (deg), ||(d||) (m), ||(a||) (m) and ||(\alpha||) (deg), separated by commas. For the joint variable (||(\theta||) of R, ||(d||) of P) write the value to draw. Lines starting with # are comments. Some exercises:
  • A planar 2R arm with links of 1 m and 0.5 m: check that with ||(\theta = (0°, 90°)||) the tool is at ||((1, 0.5, 0)||).
  • A Cartesian robot (three prismatic joints along ||(z||), ||(x||) and ||(y||)): which twists ||(\alpha_i||) make the three axes perpendicular?
  • Change the cylindrical robot of section 3 so that its last joint is vertical too. Is it still a useful robot?
